C002.subject: Foreign aid
evidence_refs: [PATH:empirical] RCTs on unconditional cash transfers (e.g., GiveDirectly) in Sub-Saharan Africa since 2010, measuring short-term poverty indices like consumption and asset accumulation — Randomized controlled trials provide high-causal evidence on whether direct foreign aid reduces poverty in the short term within the specified region and timeframe.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review of quasi-experimental studies on sectoral aid (e.g., health, agriculture) in Sub-Saharan Africa, focused on outcomes within 1-3 years of disbursement — A meta-analysis of existing quasi-experimental evidence can synthesize findings across multiple aid modalities to assess the disputed claim about short-term effectiveness.

[PATH:theoretical] CGE (computable general equilibrium) models calibrated to Sub-Saharan African economies post-2010, simulating short-run poverty impacts of foreign aid inflows — Theoretical models can clarify mechanisms (e.g., Dutch disease vs. multiplier effects) that determine whether aid reduces poverty in the short term, complementing empirical data.

C004.subject: Foreign aid
evidence_refs: [PATH:empirical] Systematic review of aid effectiveness in sub-Saharan Africa, e.g., by the Overseas Development Institute (ODI) or the World Bank's Independent Evaluation Group — Provides cross-country empirical data on post-2000 aid flows and poverty indicators, allowing analysis of correlation and causal pathways between aid dependency and persistent poverty.

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal case studies of aid-dependent countries in sub-Saharan Africa, e.g., Uganda or Malawi, focusing on governance and institutional effects — Qualitative and quantitative tracking of how aid influences local political incentives, bureaucratic capacity, and economic diversification, testing the 'entrenchment' mechanism directly.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical literature on aid dependency and poverty traps, e.g., 'The Samaritan's Dilemma' or work by William Easterly and Dambisa Moyo — Provides conceptual frameworks and causal models that predict when aid may inadvertently sustain poverty, guiding empirical tests and hypothesis refinement.
